notes.meaning: On a Sabbath, the Jewish day of rest, Jesus' disciples picked grain as they walked, rubbed off the husks in their hands, and ate it. Picking a little grain from someone's field by hand was allowed by God's law (Deuteronomy 23:25), so this was not stealing. Some older Bibles call it 'the second Sabbath after the first.' Older writers took this to mean a Sabbath soon after Passover, when the grain was ripe but not yet harvested.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many careful students of the old manuscripts think the words 'second-first' were added later by copyists. They are missing from several important manuscripts, which is why many modern Bibles simply say 'one Sabbath.'

notes.meaning: The Pharisees were strict religious teachers. They had no problem with eating grain, only with doing it on the Sabbath. By their rules, rubbing grain in your hands counted as reaping, threshing and preparing food all at once. These were man-made rules, not commands God had given.

Jesus reminded them of King David. When David and his men were hungry, they ate the holy bread that only priests were allowed to eat (1 Samuel 21:6). God's own rules about worship could give way when people were in real need. If so, human traditions could certainly give way too. David broke an actual law of Moses, while the disciples broke only a human rule.

'Son of Man' was Jesus' favorite name for Himself. By calling Himself Lord of the Sabbath, He claimed the same authority as the God who gave the law at Mount Sinai. The day of rest belongs to Him. So it is to be spent in His service and for His honor.

differ.view: Christ did not do away with the Sabbath. It continues as the Lord's Day, moved to Sunday, the first day of the week, and is still a day of rest and worship.
Christ Himself is our true rest. So the old Sabbath law is no longer binding, though Sunday is kept as the Lord's Day for worship.

notes.meaning: On another Sabbath Jesus was teaching in the synagogue, the local place of worship. He kept going there even as opposition grew. Luke, who was a doctor, notes that it was the man's right hand that was withered, meaning shrunken and useless. The man had come to hear Jesus teach.

The religious leaders watched Jesus closely, and with bad intent. They were looking for a reason to accuse Him. Their own rules allowed healing on the Sabbath only when a life was in danger. By watching, they showed they knew He could heal.

Jesus knew the hidden plans in their hearts. Instead of quietly waiting until the Sabbath was over, He called the man to stand up in front of everyone. He was not ashamed or afraid to do good in the open. This also tested the man's faith and courage.

Jesus asked a question that brought everything into the open. Is it right on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm? He teaches that to pass up a chance to do good is really to do wrong. Meanwhile, His enemies were using that very Sabbath to plan His death.

Jesus looked around at them all and told the man to stretch out his hand. He told him to do something he could not do, and gave him the power to do it. The hand was fully restored, just as it had been before. This was a true miracle, done with only a word.

Instead of being won over, the leaders were filled with a senseless rage. They were angry that they had no answer for Him. They began planning what to do to Jesus. Their plotting broke the spirit of the Sabbath far more than His healing did.

As opposition grew, Jesus went up a mountain to be alone with God. He prayed all night long. As a man, He sought His Father's guidance before an important choice. We often think half an hour of prayer is a lot, but He gave a whole night.

In the morning Jesus chose twelve of His many followers. He called them 'apostles,' which means people who are sent out with a message. Their number matched the twelve tribes of Israel, as the start of God's new people. His long prayer shows how seriously we should take choosing church leaders.

Here are the twelve, some of them brothers and fishermen. Simon 'the Zealot' was probably named for his strong zeal. Judas son of James is the one Matthew and Mark call Thaddaeus. Judas Iscariot 'became' a traitor. He showed no sign of it when chosen, yet Jesus was not fooled when He chose him.

Jesus came down with the twelve to a level place, where a huge crowd met Him. People came from Jerusalem and Judea, and even from the non-Jewish coastal cities of Tyre and Sidon. It is worth going a long way to hear Christ's word. Many writers think the sermon that follows is the same as Matthew's Sermon on the Mount, or a shorter form of it.
The people came both to hear Jesus and to be healed. Some were sick in body, and others were tormented by evil spirits. Jesus healed them all. He has power over both disease and the devil.

The whole crowd pressed in to touch Jesus, because healing power kept flowing from Him. He went on healing, one after another, until all were well. There is enough grace in Christ for everyone, and enough for each one.

Jesus looked at His disciples and spoke to them directly. 'Blessed' means truly happy in God's eyes. These were people who had left everything to follow Him, poor in this world but rich in faith. The kingdom of God, meaning God's loving rule, already belongs to them, with its full joy still to come.

differ.view: Jesus mainly means poverty of spirit, as Matthew words it: people who know they have nothing to offer and depend on God.
Luke means real, material poverty, because the poor are less tempted to trust in riches.

notes.meaning: Disciples who go hungry now and weep now are not forgotten. Their sorrows now prepare them for joy later. In the world to come they will be fully satisfied, and God will turn their tears into laughter.

Jesus warns that His followers will be hated, insulted, and even put out of the synagogue. Their very name as Christians would be treated as something evil. Yet they are blessed when this happens because they belong to Him. Jesus ties loyalty to Him together with doing what is right.

Instead of just putting up with this, they should jump for joy. A great reward waits for them in heaven. Being mistreated puts them in good company, alongside God's prophets of old who were treated the same way.

A 'woe' is a sad warning of trouble ahead. It is not aimed at every rich person, but at those who make riches their comfort and forget the life to come. They have already been 'paid in full' and have nothing more to look forward to. These words may have been spoken especially to the wealthy Pharisees.
